implementation_notes: JavaScript is the language in this catalogue where the anti-pattern is hardest to avoid, because it has neither `goto`, nor continuations, nor proper tail calls, and no labelled break — so exceptions genuinely are the only universal control-flow construct, and `throw` is the sanctioned way to exit nested loops. The honest position is that a control-flow throw is sometimes the clearest available formulation and should be a private, documented type that never escapes a module. What is not acceptable is the same mechanism used for data flow (throwing a result), and a bare `catch (e) {}` that swallows. The replacement set is generator `return`, a tagged result object, or restructuring the loop.
idiom_name: throw as a multi-level break; the only universal control-flow construct
pitfalls: `catch (e) {}` with no body swallows everything, including the control-flow sentinel and every genuine failure below it.
Promise rejection used as a non-local return from an async function, which is the async form of the same smell.
Throwing non-Error values makes control flow indistinguishable from failure and breaks `instanceof` checks downstream.
A `try` around an `await` inside `forEach` silently swallows rejections, because `forEach` does not await the returned promises.
